title: Synonyms
lines: In USAT, synonym questions give one word in capitals and four options. You choose the option closest in meaning. About four of the Verbal Reasoning questions are synonyms or antonyms, so a strong vocabulary pays off quickly. You cannot learn every word, but you can learn to work out meanings from roots, prefixes and context.
## How to attempt a synonym question
- Say the word in a short sentence of your own: "The lecture was tedious." This fixes the sense.
- Predict a simple meaning before reading the options: tedious = boring.
- Look for the option that matches your prediction; then check the others are weaker.
- If the word is unfamiliar, break it into a root and affixes and guess the direction (positive or negative, more or less).
! The closest meaning wins, not a word that is merely connected. For ARID, "desert" is related but not a synonym; "dry" is.
| voc, vok | call, voice | vocal, invoke
| in-, im-, un-, dis- | not | inaudible, impartial

Suffixes tell you the word class: -ous, -ive, -ful and -al make adjectives (cautious, decisive), -ity, -ness and -tion make nouns (scarcity, tidiness), and -ify and -ize make verbs (simplify, minimize). The synonym usually belongs to the same class as the stem word.
> A frugal person spends little and avoids waste, so frugal means thrifty: B. Generous is close to the opposite, and wealthy is about having money, not using it carefully.
> bene = good, vol = wish. A benevolent person wishes others well, so the answer is kind: A.
> A candid remark is honest and open: frank, B. Do not confuse candid with candy; and secretive is the opposite.

Many words share a general idea but differ in strength or use. Big, large, huge and colossal all mean size, but colossal is far stronger than big. If the stem word is strong, prefer the strong option. Likewise, thrifty (positive) and stingy (negative) both describe careful spending, but they carry different feelings. Match the tone as well as the meaning.
| very large | enormous, colossal, immense, vast
| lasting a short time | transient, fleeting, ephemeral

Keep a small notebook or phone list. Each time you meet a new word in a newspaper editorial or a practice question, write it with a short sentence and one synonym. Revise the list every few days and group words by idea, as in the table above. Ten new words a day for two months gives you about 600 words, which covers most of what USAT tests.
! A word may have several meanings. GRAVE can mean serious (a grave mistake) or a burial place. If the options include "serious", that is the sense being tested.
! Avoid look-alike words: eminent (famous) and imminent (about to happen); credible (believable) and credulous (too ready to believe).
! Watch the part of speech: for the adjective ABUNDANT, choose plentiful, not plenty.
- Use the word in your own sentence, then predict a meaning.
- Use roots and prefixes to judge direction when unsure.
- Match the strength, tone and word class of the stem.
- Choose the closest meaning, not a related idea.
